title: Sekigahara: Did Ieyasu Really Fire to Make Kobayakawa Defect?
description:
Keichō 5, 9th month, 15th day (October 21, 1600, Gregorian): thick fog over Sekigahara. Today's story says Ieyasu ordered shots fired at Mt. Matsuo, and only then did Kobayakawa Hideaki turn on his allies. Was that shot ever fired?

The letters from that year we have found do not mention it: Ieyasu's same-day victory report to Date Masamune (which exaggerates), Kikkawa Hiroie's draft letter ("crushed at once"), Konoe Sakihisa's letter ("won at once"), a copy of a joint report by two of Ieyasu's officers two days later, and Ieyasu's thank-you letter to Hideaki of the 24th ("just as agreed from the start"). The earliest account we have found is Ueki Etsu's Keichō Gunki (a manuscript copy, preface dated Kanbun 3, 1663; another copy has a Kanbun 8 preface), where one shot works. Kaibara Ekiken's 1684 memo has no shot; the Kuroda Kafu, finished around 1688, has a shot that does nothing; the Kuroda Kiryaku makes it a prearranged blank signal. The compiler of the 1713 Sekigahara Gunki Taisei was unsure himself. The Tokugawa Jikki appendix and the Army General Staff's 1893 Nihon Senshi made the one-shot version the standard one.

Verdict: the shot is filed. No contemporary letter we have found has it, and most researchers (Shiramine Jun, Goza Yūichi, Takahashi Yōsuke) see it as a later invention, while Kasaya Kazuhiko holds back. When Hideaki turned is still open.

"Age 19" counts years the old way and follows recent research dating his birth to 1582; another view says 1577. The joint report and Konoe's letter are partly read as quoted by Japanese Wikipedia and printed editions, not the originals, and we read only one copy of the Keichō Gunki. Narration dates use the old lunar calendar; sentences beginning "we think" are this channel's view. Sources are in the references below.

Illustrations are AI-generated; historical figures are unnamed cartoon characters, not likenesses. Modern researchers and the fighting are not drawn.

Information as of 2026-10-20

sk101.text: Keichō 5, month 9, day 15: light rain, thick fog at Sekigahara.

sk102.text: Ieyasu's physician wrote: at its thickest, you couldn't see past 90 meters.

sk103.text: In the fog, only a roar of gunfire.

sk104.text: Kobayakawa Hideaki had taken 10,000-plus men up Mt. Matsuo the day before.

sk105.text: By recent research, he was 19 that year.

sk106.text: The story today: Ieyasu, impatient, orders shots fired up the hill;

sk107.text: at the shot, Hideaki defects and charges down.

sk108.text: Yet after the battle, Ieyasu wrote to thank Hideaki. Thank him for what?

sk109.text: Stranger still, a later war tale has Ieyasu bite through his nails.

sk110.text: A Confucian historian of the Kuroda wrote this battle up three times.

sk111.text: And one compiler put a question mark in his own book.

sk112.text: Did Ieyasu really fire on Mt. Matsuo?

sk201.text: Battle over, Ieyasu wrote a victory note.

sk202.text: It went to Date Masamune, and the original letter survives.

sk203.text: It says: today around noon, we fought at Yamanaka in Nōshū and wiped out the enemy.

sk204.text: It adds he reached Sawayama that day and took Ōgaki.

sk205.text: In fact, that night Ieyasu moved to Yamanaka village; Ōgaki Castle surrendered later.

sk206.text: A victory report that says too much, and it never mentions Hideaki.

sk207.text: So what did people elsewhere hear?

sk208.text: Kikkawa Hiroie's troops sat on Mt. Nangū that day, unmoving.

sk209.text: His later draft letter notes what he heard:

sk210.text: As expected, at Yamanaka they were routed at once.

sk211.text: On the 20th, in Kyoto, Konoe Sakihisa heard Ieyasu's men out and wrote too:

sk212.text: Won in an instant; then Kingo switched sides.

sk213.text: Kingo means Hideaki. And what did Hideaki himself receive?

sk214.text: That thank-you letter is dated the 24th, addressed to Hideaki himself:

sk215.text: As agreed from the start; I am very glad.

sk216.text: All thanks; not one word urging him on.

sk217.text: So when exactly did Hideaki defect?

sk218.text: Two days on, two of Ieyasu's officers sent a report; what survives is a copy.

sk219.text: They weren't at the front line themselves.

sk220.text: It says when the armies clashed, four men, Kobayakawa among them, turned; the enemy broke.

sk221.text: Researcher Shiramine Jun reads "when they clashed" as the battle's start.

sk222.text: But was the clash the first moment, or the middle of the fight?

sk223.text: Five letters read. Where does the shot at Mt. Matsuo first appear?

sk301.text: The earliest we've found is Ueki Etsu's Keichō Gunki, prefaced in the 1st month of Kanbun 3.

sk302.text: The preface ends: respectfully written in a grove in Suruga.

sk303.text: It spread in handwritten copies; one copy's preface says Kanbun 8.

sk304.text: It says Hideaki hid his defection even from his chief retainers; troops knew nothing.

sk305.text: But the battle had begun, and no one knew if the men on Mt. Matsuo were friend or foe.

sk307.text: Frantic, he bit off his left-hand nails and, agitated, ordered:

sk309.text: On the order, Tōdō and Kyōgoku foot soldiers fired toward the hill.

sk310.text: And Hideaki up on the hill?

sk311.text: His troops stirred, then re-formed ranks,

sk312.text: then, with four other units, wheeled on Ōtani Yoshitsugu's camp.

sk313.text: In this book, the shot works from the start.

sk314.text: Twenty-odd years later, a Fukuoka Confucian told this battle too.

sk401.text: Kaibara Ekiken, Confucian historian of the Kuroda of Fukuoka.

sk402.text: In Jōkyō 1, in Edo, he briefed two Confucians on the Kuroda and left a memo.

sk403.text: It says: mid-battle, with no winner in sight and the enemy's banners riding high,

sk404.text: Hideaki, as agreed, led his army charging down Mt. Matsuo.

sk407.text: the Kuroda credit Hideaki's turn to Kuroda Nagamasa;

sk408.text: yet none of the popular books mention it.

sk409.text: And the Kuroda genealogy he compiled?

sk410.text: The Kuroda Kafu was done around Genroku 1; this time, the shot appears.

sk411.text: A rider in black tells Ieyasu: Hideaki's banners may be friend or foe.

sk412.text: Ieyasu has 20 Fukushima gunners fire two volleys at Mt. Matsuo.

sk414.text: Still, Hideaki's men stayed up the hill.

sk415.text: Retainer Hiraoka Iwami: "Too early. I'm waiting."

sk416.text: When Shima Sakon's line, on Ishida's side, broke, he waved his baton: charge!

sk417.text: Stranger still is the third telling, in his undated Kuroda Kiryaku.

sk418.text: This time the gunners go from 20 to 50, firing blanks.

sk419.text: The book guesses it was a prearranged signal.

sk420.text: Seeing it, Hiraoka said: the time is right, attack.

sk421.text: The compiler with the question mark was Miyagawa Naofuru; his Sekigahara Gunki Taisei dates to Shōtoku 3.

sk422.text: On retainers Hiraoka and Inaba, he stops to ask:

sk423.text: Scared by those shots? Or timing it all along?

sk425.text: He even doubts the shooters: Fukushima's camp was far from Mt. Matsuo. Why them?

sk426.text: He adds another version: Tōdō's camp fired, as in the Keichō Gunki.

sk427.text: In the 19th century, the shogunate's own history took it up.

sk501.text: It's the Tokugawa Jikki appendix: the version where one shot works.

sk502.text: Told Hideaki's banners looked doubtful, Ieyasu's face changed:

sk504.text: He had probing shots fired below the hill; at the sound, Hideaki's troops finally came down.

sk505.text: It cites the Tengen Jikki for this.

sk506.text: So the opening story entered the shogunate's own history.

sk507.text: In Meiji 26, the Army General Staff put out Nihon Senshi: Sekigahara.

sk508.text: It says that near noon, the outcome was still unclear;

sk509.text: two gunner units volleyed at Mt. Matsuo on orders; only then did Hideaki give the word.

sk510.text: A tale from Edo books became the army's official history.

sk512.text: In Shōwa 11, a teachers' guide wrote: fog so thick you couldn't see a foot ahead;

sk513.text: Ieyasu fired at Mt. Matsuo; only then did Hideaki resolve to charge.

sk514.text: We think each time this shot is written, the fog gets a bit thicker.

sk516.text: Later it was named toi-deppō, the "asking shot."

sk517.text: In 2013, Shiramine Jun combed these Edo books and concluded it isn't fact,

sk518.text: but invented amid the Edo-era deification of Ieyasu.

sk519.text: Some reserve judgment: Kasaya Kazuhiko says Hideaki's wavering isn't pure fiction.

sk520.text: Remember "when they clashed" in that copy?

sk521.text: Shiramine says the very start; Kasaya says Hideaki waited till near noon.

sk522.text: So, the opening question: did Ieyasu really fire?

sk523.text: This shot was first fired on paper, more than 60 years later.

sk524.text: The shot: case filed. When Hideaki turned: still open.

sk525.text: Which version did you hear first?

sk526.text: We tell only what records show. Subscribe to open the files with us.
